display_title: Official Review of Paper1782 by Reviewer p1tx

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for improving tasks relying on common sense by generating knowledge graph paths to provide additional context to QA systems. it is evaluated on a variety of tasks achieving strong results.
content.main_review:
The results in the paper are good, but it is unclear why. As mentioned in section 4.3, the method proposed is a modification of the path generation component of Wang et al. (2020b), but otherwise the same. Wang et al, also used a pretrained LM fine tuned on KG triples, thus most of the motivation is the same. The only difference as far as I can tell, is the use of a different pretrained LM (T5 instead of GPT2), and possibly in the training data generation. However, the paper doesn't try to explain what the differences are, so it is unclear why the results are better. The masking might be novel, but it seems not to have much of an impact on the results (Table 3). On the whole though, it appears to be a better implementation of Wang et al. (2020b), but the ideas are the same, so I don't think another paper is warranted.

A couple of other points:
- In the evaluation of the triples, I think novelty should also take into account whether the triple is actually correct; not just that it doesn't appear in training
- Finally, the paper is poorly written, with a lot of grammar errors and poor phrasings such as "to scale the knowledge" (abstract), "model has to classify correct choice" (introduction), etc. thus better proofreading is needed.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the results are positive, the paper does not justify why the method proposed improves on previous work, and in particular work also performing path generation.

content.title: Response to Reviewer p1tx
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments and feedback.

***

> Wang et al, also used a pretrained LM fine tuned on KG triples, thus most of the motivation is the same. The only difference as far as I can tell, is the use of a different pretrained LM (T5 instead of GPT2), and possibly in the training data generation. However, the paper doesn't try to explain what the differences are, so it is unclear why the results are better.

We would like to highlight that we design CoSe-Co with the aim of developing a **task-agnostic** generic commonsense generator that takes into account the **overall context** of the input text. Conditioning on sentences as input to generate relevant commonsense enables us to apply CoSe-Co across various tasks. On the other hand, PGQA (Wang et al. (2020b)) is designed **specifically for multi-choice QA** and relies on answer choice and entity extraction for commonsense generation. It extracts entities from text and generates commonsense between entities and answer choices **independent of the overall question context** which is a major drawback (as discussed in the introduction and related work sections). We would like to motivate why context is crucial through an example from CSQA dataset:

Consider the question  - **‘Where could you see an advertisement while reading news?’**. PGQA extracts ‘reading news’ from the question, considers it as the source entity, and pairs it up with a candidate choice ‘television’ as the target entity to generate the path - ```‘read_news  hassubevent  read  relatedto  news  atlocation  television’``` ignoring the context that advertisement is being seen along with reading news and hence it ends up predicting television as answer which is wrong. On the other hand, CoSe-Co takes the question as input and generates the path - ```‘spread_information  _capableof advertisement  atlocation  web_page  usedfor  reading_news’```. Here it can be seen that CoSe-Co considers the entire sentence context, uses the understanding that seeing the advertisement and reading news is happening together and generates path accordingly to relate them with ‘web page’ which is the correct answer (more of such qualitative examples and comparison were provided in Appendix A). This highlights the fact that considering overall context is crucial and generating commonsense while ignoring this context is a major drawback of PGQA which needs to be addressed.

To address these limitations, we propose CoSe-Co and train it over semantically related sentence-commonsense pairs that enable it to generate contextually more relevant and useful commonsense. In order to train CoSe-Co, we need a dataset comprising of pairs of natural language sentences and associated commonsense inferences. To create the dataset, we first sample paths from an underlying commonsense KG, and then retrieve sentences from a sentence corpus that are semantically relevant and related to a sampled path. We then use this dataset to train CoSe-Co to generate contextually relevant commonsense paths given an input sentence.

continued...

content.title: Response to Reviewer p1tx (continued)
content.comment:
Further, any generative LM can be used as the backbone for CoSe-Co. Using T5-base was simply a design choice, since it is a text-to-text generation language model. To empirically establish that performance gains over PGQA (GPT-2 based) are not due to using T5-base instead of GPT-2, we performed an experiment to replace T5-base with GPT-2 as the backbone language model of CoSe-Co. We train GPT-2 using the same sentence-path dataset as we used for T5-base by providing it as input the sentence followed by a [SEP] token and adapting GPT-2 to generate the corresponding path. Additionally, we also experiment with replacing the language model in PGQA from GPT-2 to T5-base. The following table summarises the results obtained for multi-choice QA on CSQA:

| Method                     | IHDev     | IHTest     |               |
|------------------------    |-------    |--------    |------------    |
| RoBERTa-large (w/o KG)                  | 73.07 (±0.45)| 68.69 (±0.56) |
| + PGQA (w/ GPT-2)          | 77.53 (±0.47) | 71.19 (±0.49) |
| + CoSe-Co (w/ GPT-2)       | **77.90** (±0.37) | **72.67** (±0.18) |
|                            |           |            |                |
| + PGQA (w/ T5-base)        | 77.56 (±0.32) | 71.31 (±0.44) |
| + CoSe-Co (w/ T5-base)     | **78.15** (±0.23) | **72.87** (±0.31) |

It can be seen that using GPT-2 vs T5 do not lead to noticeable changes in the performance. The test accuracy attained by CoSe-Co with T5-base is 72.87% which is almost the same as for CoSe-Co with GPT-2: 72.67%. A similar observation is seen for PGQA where using T5-base backbone gives 71.31% and using GPT-2 gives 71.19%. Further, we would like to highlight that CoSe-Co with GPT-2 backbone attains 72.67% accuracy and performs better than PGQA with GPT-2 (71.19%). We have also added these results to appendix C. 

Based on these observations, we can conclude that the performance gains of CoSe-Co over PGQA are not due to using a different backbone but because CoSe-Co is trained over semantically related sentence-commonsense pairs that enables it to generate contextually more relevant and useful commonsense.

*** 
> As mentioned in section 4.3, the method proposed is a modification of the path generation component of Wang et al. (2020b), but otherwise the same

We would like to emphasize that our aim in the paper is not to design an improved QA module but instead we design CoSe-Co with the aim of developing a generic task-agnostic commonsense generator that takes into account the overall context of the text (a major drawback of prior works). In section 4.3, we consider multi-choice QA as one of the tasks to evaluate CoSe-Co where we compare it with one of the prior works - PGQA which is designed specifically for multi-choice QA. Hence, for fair and uniform comparison with PGQA, we use their proposed QA module and just inject commonsense inferences generated by CoSe-Co (instead of PGQA paths). This is to establish and highlight that performance gains over PGQA are due to the reason that CoSe-Co generates contextually more relevant and useful commonsense (due to the differences discussed earlier in our response) and not due to using a different/modified QA module.

***
> In the evaluation of the triples, I think novelty should also take into account whether the triple is actually correct; not just that it doesn't appear in training

As discussed in section 4.2, along with novelty, we also estimated **relevance** to measure the degree of correctness of triples in the generated paths on the test split of sentence-path dataset. To estimate this measure, we treat one triple in a path as one uni-gram. Following this scheme, the generated and ground truth paths can be viewed as a sequence of uni-grams. We then calculate the BLEU score between them. CoSe-Co achieves a relevance score of **0.436** along with a novelty of 23.28% which shows that the generated paths are accurate since the triples match with the ground truth path as well as a good number of entities in each generated path are novel on an average. It should be noted that since there could be a diverse set of commonsense inferences associated with a given sentence, a relevance score of 0.436 (on a scale of 0 to 1) is very good. 

***
> Finally, the paper is poorly written, with a lot of grammar errors and poor phrasings such as "to scale the knowledge" (abstract), "model has to classify correct choice" (introduction), etc. thus better proofreading is needed.

We have now made the suggested changes in the phrasing and have performed thorough proofreading in the updated version of the paper.

***

content.title: Response to Reviewer's Reply
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for the response.

***

**Human Evaluation** : To study the difference in the quality of generated commonsense between CoSe-Co and PGQA, we conducted a human evaluation and found that knowledge generated by CoSe-Co is significantly more contextually relevant than PGQA. For human study, we presented evaluators with questions from CSQA dataset along with corresponding commonsense paths generated by CoSe-Co and PGQA in an anonymized manner. We asked them to compare the paths based on their contextual relevance with the complete sentence and usefulness in answering the question and rate which path is better. We also provided them an option to mark neutral in case none of the paths is clearly better than the other for a given sample. A total of 150 questions samples were randomly sampled from the test set and presented to 6 evaluators (25 samples each). Following are our observations:

* Number of samples where CoSe-Co is better: 62 (41.33% of 150 samples)
* Number of samples where PGQA is better: 38 (25.33% of 150 samples)
* Number of samples where both are of similar quality: 50 (33.33% of 150 samples)
 
This shows that commonsense generated by CoSe-Co is found to be more relevant in human evaluation. Also, if we exclude neutral samples and consider the 100 samples where the path generated by one of the two methods is found to be better, CoSe-Co’s paths are found to be more relevant in 62 samples (62% of 100 samples) while PGQA’s paths are more relevant in 38 samples (38% of 100 samples). We have now added this human study to qualitative analysis in Appendix A in the updated draft.

***

**Correctness of Novel Triples** : Since there is no ground truth to check the correctness of triple comprising of novel entities, we attempt to evaluate them by leveraging a commonsense knowledge base completion model - Bilinear AVG [1] which has been shown to achieve an accuracy of 92.5% on knowledge completion task and is also used to score triples. We extract triples comprising of at least one novel entity from the paths generated by CoSe-Co for the test split of sentence-path dataset and provide the triple to Bilinear AVG to obtain a score. The average score over all the triples is **0.414** (on a scale of 0 to 1).


[1] Xiang Li, Aynaz Taheri, Lifu Tu, and Kevin Gimpel. 2016. Commonsense knowledge base completion. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 1445–1455.

content.title: Experiments on General Applicability of CoSe-Co in Tasks
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the response.

To highlight the generality of CoSe-Co, we added the paraphrase text generation experiment on MRPC dataset back to the main paper where augmenting knowledge generated by CoSe-Co results in up to ~1.5% improvement in generation metrics (Section 4.5 and Table 5 in the current pdf). For this task and dataset, the entities are not available and hence PGQA is not applicable. This shows that CoSe-Co can also be used in NLP tasks where entities are not available to achieve performance gains since it is designed to be conditioned on text sentences. This generality is another key difference and advantage in addition to using the entire text context to generate more relevant commonsense.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose CoSe-Co, a generative model that generates relevant commonsense knowledge paths from a given natural language input sentence. First, the authors develop a new sentence to KG-path dataset curation technique and use ConceptNet to create a large dataset to finetune T5. After fine-tuning, this model can be essentially used as a source of commonsense knowledge for any sentence. Through experiments on multiple datasets, the authors establish that such a model is able to generate some meaningful knowledge and novel concepts that help solve downstream tasks more efficiently.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
Overall, the paper is quite well motivated and easy to read. Technically, the input format for CoSe-Co indeed makes it easier to apply to downstream tasks, which was a limitation of many prior works. Additionally, the dataset created by the authors can be a helpful resource as well. Lastly, diverse-path search is a good inductive bias for path decoding and would be relevant to the related community.

Weaknesses/Questions:
* On possible data leakage - Current models use ConceptNet as the KG which is probably fine (although it is a source of data leakage for CSQA dataset). Apart from that, you're also using Wikipedia for sentence selection. Do you perform any checks on data overlap with the training set of CoSe-Co? I think this can lead to wrong conclusions if not addressed correctly.
* On querying partial paths - In this case, will the training data consist of sentence and the partial path that matched, or the complete path even though it was not used to match? If the latter, I wonder if that makes the dataset too noisy?
* On ER-templates - The motivation for Q1 is not clear. Why are $(e_i, r_i, e_{i+2})$ and $(e_i, r_{i+1}, e_{i+2})$ chosen as templates? Please add some intuitions on why these were chosen (other than the ablation). Did you also try some other formats that did not work?
* On diverse-path search - Do you mean only first entity is important? I believe any entity once selected can guide the path generation, with importance decreasing as the path length increases. So, even 2nd and 3rd entities could be quite important to decide the path direction. Or did you find that's not the case?
* On choice of $l_1$ - Is there any reason $l_1 < 3$ was not chosen? 2-hop paths can be meaningful and also abundant.
* On diversity - Isn't the metric used very noisy? Also, this is probably biased to generating just different lengths instead of diverse texts. If this has already been used for some diversity evaluation of sentences, please add those references.
* On CSQA baselines - Please add some T5 baseline to the table, otherwise the comparison is probably not fair.

Needs clarity:
* Please add some running example or illustration to explain the sentence-path paired dataset creation. Currently, the para is bit hard to parse and an example will make it easier to understand.
* Please mention more details on the baseline method PGQA in appendix. I'd suggest adding a brief para explaining the working of the model and also clarifying how the heuristic filtering works for relations.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has interesting contributions in terms of the new training dataset + model proposed. Through many experiments the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their method. But, some concerns about data leakage need to be addressed to ensure the gains are rightly attributed. Overall, I'm leaning towards acceptance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer MgN3 (1/3)
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments and feedback.

***

> On possible data leakage - Current models use ConceptNet as the KG which is probably fine (although it is a source of data leakage for CSQA dataset). Apart from that, you're also using Wikipedia for sentence selection. Do you perform any checks on data overlap with the training set of CoSe-Co? I think this can lead to wrong conclusions if not addressed correctly.

We determine the extent of n-gram overlap between questions in the CSQA test set and sentences in our sentence-path training set as indicators of leakage. For this, we obtain the set of n-grams in a question, determine the sentence in the training set with which the question has maximum matching n-grams and divide the matching n-gram count with the total number of n-grams in the question. Finally, this fraction is averaged over all the questions in the test split of CSQA. Following this scheme, an overlap of 0.15 is observed for 1-grams, 0.07 for 2-grams, 0.002 for 3-grams, and 0.00 for 4-grams which shows that the extent of overlap is very less (on a scale of 0 to 1). Further, we noted that 1-gram overlap does not necessarily indicate leakage. For instance, consider CSQA test question - *‘If a person is tired how can they be refreshed?’*. Even though, it has matching 1-grams with the sentence- ‘a person may feel tired without having engaged in any physical activity’, but it can be noted that they have an entirely different context. From the low n-gram overlap values, we conclude that the extent of leakage is negligible.

Upon receiving your feedback, we thought further about the leakage concerns which we would like to discuss here: To create the sentence-path paired data, we use a Wikipedia sentences corpus [1], which is a subset of the commonly used corpora to pre-train language models such as BERT, RoBERTa, etc. These pre-trained language models are commonly used for transfer learning and obtaining useful embedded representations of text by various prior works in different downstream tasks including multi-choice QA on CSQA dataset. For instance, PGQA and QA-GNN use RoBERTa to embed the question and choices. Hence, training CoSe-Co over sentence-path pairs obtained using just a subset of Wikipedia corpus (since eventually, we obtain a total of ~290K sentence-path pairs) would cause much lesser leakage than caused by using language models to embed the question and choices text for tasks like multi-choice QA.

[1] https://archive.org/download/enwiki-20181220

*** 
> On querying partial paths - In this case, will the training data consist of sentence and the partial path that matched, or the complete path even though it was not used to match? If the latter, I wonder if that makes the dataset too noisy?

The training dataset consists of the entire path (with the matched sentences) and not only the partial path that is used to create the query to retrieve sentences. We specifically made this choice to enable CoSe-Co to learn to generate not only the entities that are explicitly present in the sentence but also other entities that are semantically related to the context of the sentence through commonsense but not present in the sentence. To minimize the noise, after retrieving the relevant sentences with the partial path as query, we also perform a second step where we compute the similarity between the embeddings (obtained using S-BERT) of retrieved sentences and corresponding queries and rank sentences based on similarity score across all the queries. We then retain only the top K’ sentences based on the ranking and filter out the remaining ones. We cap the maximum number of sentences per path to K’ = 10 to prevent CoSe-Co from getting biased towards generating a particular path.

Further, to gauge the degree of noise in the dataset and relevance between the final set of sentence-path pairs, we measure the cosine similarity between the S-BERT embeddings of the complete path and the corresponding sentence in the dataset. We observe a **high normalized cosine similarity score of 0.783** when averaged over all sentence-path pairs in the training dataset which shows that sentence and corresponding path pairs are semantically related.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer MgN3 (1/3)

content.title: Response to Reviewer MgN3 (2/3)
content.comment:
*** 
> On ER-templates - The motivation for Q1 is not clear. Why are $(e_i, r_i, e_{i+2})$ and $(e_i, r_{i+1}, e_{i+2})$ chosen as templates? Please add some intuitions on why these were chosen (other than the ablation). Did you also try some other formats that did not work?

We chose the two templates after observing different kinds of queries and retrieved sentences. We observed and had two intuitions for using these templates:
* For extracting sentences that are relevant to the overall path

Given a path $(e_1, r_1, e_2, r_2, …, e_n)$, using non-contiguous entities to obtain partial path according to query templates such as $(e_i, r_i, e_{i+2})$ and $(e_i, r_{i+1}, e_{i+2})$ enables us to retrieve sentences that are relatively more related to the overall path. Two contiguous entities (as in our Q2 template) in a path are often very directly related to each other and only using them as a query could retrieve sentences that are irrelevant or unrelated to most parts of the path that are not in the query. 

For instance, consider a path ```‘violin  hasproperty  strings  _hasprequistite  guitar  atlocation  concert’```. If we would use a query {violin, hasproperty, strings} (of the contiguous form $(e_i, r_i, e_{i+1})$), then a number of sentences containing ‘violin’ and ‘strings’ with no relatedness with the larger path context (such as 'concert') could be retrieved. However, queries like {strings, atlocation, concert’} (of the form $(e_i, r_{i+1}, e_{i+2})$) following our Q1 template are more likely to retrieve sentences that are more semantically related with the whole path (given a sentence containing ‘string and ‘concert’, it is more likely that the sentence context is related to other entities in the path such as ‘guitar’).

* For better inductive biases in CoSe-Co

In ConceptNet and related commonsense knowledge graphs, many pairs of non-neighboring entities (which are not directly related) in a path are connected through some intermediate entities. We retrieve sentences that contain entities that are not directly related in the corresponding path and subsequently train CoSe-Co to learn to generate the path comprising of intermediate entities which connect them (essentially interpolate between entities). It would induce an inductive bias in CoSe-Co to generate paths that connect entities in a given sentence using commonsense.

We have now modified section 3.1 to include the above intuitions behind choosing the query templates.

*** 

> On diverse-path search - Do you mean only first entity is important? I believe any entity once selected can guide the path generation, with importance decreasing as the path length increases. So, even 2nd and 3rd entities could be quite important to decide the path direction. Or did you find that's not the case?

We did not intend to suggest that only the first entity is important. We wanted to convey that choosing k most probable tokens at the first decoding step results in generating different first entities which in turn helps in decoding diverse paths. In the paper, we only tried diverse-path-search at the first decoding step since it was the most natural choice to influence the entire path generation. However, we do agree that diverse-path search can further be applied at different steps and for different entities (2nd, 3rd etc.) during decoding to influence the subsequent path sequence being generated.

***

> On choice of $l_1$- Is there any reason $l_1 < 3$ was not chosen? 2-hop paths can be meaningful and also abundant.

In the original draft, we defined path length |p| as the number of entities in the path. Hence, the number of hops in a path is |p| - 1 accordinging to that definition. The range of 3 to 6 for path length corresponded to the range 2 to 5 for the number of hops. We indeed sample 2-hop paths while creating our dataset. Moreover, we did not sample triples (1-hop paths) to ensure that paths being sampled are sufficiently informative to expand the commonsense context of the sentence, thus keeping the lower limit on hops as 2. We realised that our definition of path length should be changed to number of hops for better clarity to avoid confusion and we have now made this change in the updated paper (section 3.1 and 4.1).

content.title: Response to Reviewer MgN3 (3/3)
content.comment:
***
> On diversity - Isn't the metric used very noisy? Also, this is probably biased to generating just different lengths instead of diverse texts. If this has already been used for some diversity evaluation of sentences, please add those references.

To probe the noise concern due to path length bias, we measure the standard deviation of the number of entities in paths generated corresponding to test split sentences and found it to be 0.76 which shows that variance in the lengths of generated paths is very low ($<1$) and hence, the diversity of 0.43 (on a scale 0 to 1) attained by CoSe-Co is not due to length bias. 

We defined the diversity metric ourselves to measure this attribute for paths and to study the influence of diverse-path search. 

***
> On CSQA baselines - Please add some T5 baseline to the table, otherwise the comparison is probably not fair.

We have now added T5-base and T5-large as additional baselines for CSQA in Table 2. For reference, the observations are also shown in the table below. 

| Method                 	| IHDev 	| IHTest 	|
|------------------------	|-------	|--------	|
| T5-base (w/o KG)       	|  61.88 (±0.08) 	|  57.34 (±0.21)   |
| T5-large (w/o KG)      	|   69.81 (±1.02) 	|  67.80 (±0.83)  |
|	|	|	|
| RoBERTa-large (w/o KG) 	| 73.07 (±0.45)	| 68.69 (±0.56) 	|
| + CoSe-Co              	| 78.15 (±0.23)	| 72.87 (±0.31)	|

***
> Please add some running example or illustration to explain the sentence-path paired dataset creation. Currently, the para is bit hard to parse and an example will make it easier to understand.

We have now added figure 3 (section 3.1) in the updated version of the paper to demonstrate the creation of sentence-path paired data creation through illustrations for each step.

***
> Please mention more details on the baseline method PGQA in appendix. I'd suggest adding a brief para explaining the working of the model and also clarifying how the heuristic filtering works for relations.

We have now added further details of PGQA method in appendix D and relation heuristics for path filtering have been added to appendix F.1.

***

I thank the authors for carefully addressing my concerns regarding the dataset curation details and baseline concerns. Given the current state, I'll keep my recommendation unchanged.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a task agonistic CommonSense Contextualizer(CoSe-Co) to generate diverse and novel knowledge paths relevant to given sentences as input. They create new sentence-commonsense path paired data to train CoSe-Co. CoSe-Co generates paths that contain novel entities not present in KG. It demonstrates that their method outperforms current SOTA models on Multi-Choice QA and OpenCSR tasks and further results in better performance with low training data.
content.main_review:
Strengths
1. CoSe-Co achieves new SOTA results on Multi-Choice QA and OpenCSR.
2. CoSe-Co outperforms PGQA and generates better commonsense paths showing in Appendix A.
3. The authors perform thorough experiments and ablation studies to demonstrate effectiveness of their method.

Weaknesses/Questions
1. When creating sentence-path paired dataset, they query Solr and rank retrieved sentences based on similarity between sentence embedding and embedded representation of the query. Does that mean you filter the retrieved sentences based on the ranking? More explanation would be helpful.
2. In 4.1, they set the length of paths in the range of 3 and 6. Just wondering if they explore other ranges. 
3. In 4.2, it mentions that CoSe-Co attained a novelty of 23.28%. How do you measure such novelty? Do authors read some examples and calculate the fractions and are 23.28% enough for a good fraction?
4. In figure 3 (b), the greedy decoding result is missed. Since the BLEU scores for greedy decoding and diverse-path search are the same, it would be useful to see how different they are in diversity measurement.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, the proposed method seems to be reasonable and outperforms existing methods. Their proposed framework, CoSe-Co achieves new SOTA on Multi-Choice QA and OpenCSR and they create sentence-path paired dataset that did not exist before. However, there are some points that they have not specified in the paper which I write down in the main review above.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1782 by Reviewer 97zu

content.title: Response to Reviewer 97zu
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments and feedback.

***

> When creating sentence-path paired dataset, they query Solr and rank retrieved sentences based on similarity between sentence embedding and embedded representation of the query. Does that mean you filter the retrieved sentences based on the ranking? More explanation would be helpful.

Yes, we retain only the top K’ sentences based on the ranking and filter out the remaining ones. We cap the maximum number of sentences per path to K’ = 10 to prevent CoSe-Co from getting biased towards generating a particular path. Ranking and filtering also ensure that only the most semantically relevant sentences to the path are retained while creating the sentence-path pairs. Thanks for bringing this to our notice, we have now improved this explanation in the paper (Section 3.1). 

***

> In 4.1, they set the length of paths in the range of 3 and 6. Just wondering if they explore other ranges.

In the original draft, we defined path length |p| as the number of entities in the path. Hence, the number of hops in a path is |p| - 1. We constrain the path length in the range 3 to 6, which is equivalent to limiting number of hops in the range 2 to 5. To ensure that paths being sampled are sufficiently informative to expand the commonsense context of a sentence, we do not sample triples (number of hops = 1). Hence, the lower limit on hops is kept as 2. Further, we observed that on increasing the hops to a large number, the entities which are far apart in a long path tend to be unrelated. As an example, the tail entitiy ```‘cave’``` is mostly unrelated to the entity ```‘apologize’``` in the long path- ```"apologize _haslastsubevent  hurt_else  causes  guilt  hasfirstsubevent  say_sorry  _hasprerequisite  forgive  _hasproperty  monk  atlocation  cave"```. Hence, we limit the maximum number of hops to 5. Since our original definition of path length (as the number of entities) caused confusion, we have now made changes to the paper (in section 3.1 and section 4.1) to re-define it as number of hops which is one less than number of entities.

***

> In 4.2, it mentions that CoSe-Co attained a novelty of 23.28%. How do you measure such novelty? Do authors read some examples and calculate the fractions and are 23.28% enough for a good fraction?

We programmatically estimate the novelty over the test split of <sentence, path> dataset and not by judging through reading just a few examples. For this, we provide sentences in the test split (comprising of 11,264 sentence-path pairs) as input to the trained CoSe-Co model and generate the paths. We extract the entities in a generated path and determine the count of entities that are not present in the set of entities in any of the training paths. For a given generated path, we estimate the proportion of such novel entities over the total number of entities in the path and take the average over all the samples in the test set. We believe 23.28% is a good fraction since it indicates that approximately one-fourth of the total entities in a generated path are novel. We have now enhanced the definition of novelty in section 4.2. 

***

> In figure 3 (b), the greedy decoding result is missed. Since the BLEU scores for greedy decoding and diverse-path search are the same, it would be useful to see how different they are in diversity measurement.

The greedy decoding technique generates only a **single unique path**. This is because it selects a single token with maximum likelihood at every generation step and conditions the subsequent decoding on them while generating the path tokens sequentially. Since only a single path is obtained using greedy decoding, it is not possible to estimate diversity for this technique. This is not the case with other decoding strategies shown in figure 3 (a) and figure 3 (b), that can be used to generate multiple paths per sentence.

***

replying_to: Replying to CoSe-Co: Text Conditioned Generative CommonSense Contextualizer
display_title: Official Review of Paper1782 by Reviewer TrPL

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a CommonSense Contextualizer (CoSe-Co) to generate the commonsense knowledge that can be augmented in downstream tasks, such as multi-choice QA, open-ended QA to improve the performance. 

The key idea is: 1) train a generative LM (i.e., CoSe-Co) on their collected <sentence, commonsense path> pairs data; 2) utilize it to generate commonsense paths (sequences of entities connected through relations) for a given textual input in downstream tasks; 3) concatenate the textual input and corresponding generated paths as the new input to the task-specific model.

The authors release a sentence and commonsense path paired dataset collected by their devised heuristic-rule based method.

Extensive experiments show augmenting commonsense paths generated by CoSe-Co in Multi-Choice QA and OpenCSR brings the improvements over current SOTA methods.
content.main_review:
**Strengths**:

Contribute a novel dataset consisting of <sentence, commonsense path> pairs together with their collecting method.

Present a general commonsense knowledge generator trained on this dataset to generate commonsense paths that can be augmented in downstream tasks. 


**Weaknesses**:

My main concern is about the technical novelty of the proposed method. Compared to the path generator in (Wang et al., 2020b), the difference is that CoSe-Co is T5-based LM rather than GPT-2 and can take the natural sentences as input.

The claimed significant improvement on multi-choice QA is about 3%. However, experimental results in Table 2 show the improvement is only about 0.58% on test split using full training data, compared to QA-GNN. Besides, when using 60% training data, the improvement over PGQA is also incremental.

The comparison with PGQA is a bit unfair since PGQA is based on GPT-2 (trained on 40 GB text data) while CoSe-Co is based on T5-base (trained on 7 TB).



**Questions for the authors**:

In Section 4.2, the ratio of the novel entities in generated paths by CoSe-Co can reach 23.28%, which are not present in training paths. I am curious where these novel entities come from.

Did you try to change the backbone of CoSe-Co to other generative LM such as GPT-2?
content.summary_of_the_review: My recommendation is to reject this paper. The main contribution is on the empirical side and it is more suitable to the CL conferences.

content.title: Response to Reviewer TrPL (1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments and feedback.
***

> Did you try to change the backbone of CoSe-Co to other generative LM such as GPT-2?

To explore the effect of changing the backbone language model of CoSe-Co, we replace T5-base with GPT-2. We train GPT-2 using the same sentence-path dataset as we used for T5-base by providing it as input the sentence followed by a [SEP] token and adapting GPT-2 to generate the corresponding path. Additionally, we also experiment with replacing the language model in PGQA from GPT-2 to T5-base. The following table summarises the results obtained for multi-choice QA on CSQA: 

| Method                 	| IHDev 	| IHTest 	|               |
|------------------------	|-------	|--------	|------------	|
| RoBERTa-large (w/o KG)          		| 73.07 (±0.45)| 68.69 (±0.56) |
| + PGQA (w/ GPT-2)      	| 77.53 (±0.47) | 71.19 (±0.49) |
| + CoSe-Co (w/ GPT-2)   	| **77.90** (±0.37) | **72.67** (±0.18) |
|                        	|       	|        	|            	|
| + PGQA (w/ T5-base)    	| 77.56 (±0.32) | 71.31 (±0.44) | 
| + CoSe-Co (w/ T5-base) 	| **78.15** (±0.23) | **72.87** (±0.31) |

It can be seen that using GPT-2 vs T5 does not lead to noticeable changes in the performance. The test accuracy attained by CoSe-Co with T5-base is 72.87% which is almost the same as for CoSe-Co with GPT-2: 72.67%. A similar observation is seen for PGQA where using T5-base backbone gives 71.31% and using GPT-2 gives 71.19%. Further, we would like to highlight that CoSe-Co with GPT-2 backbone attains 72.67% accuracy and performs better than PGQA with GPT-2 (71.19%). We thank the reviewer for suggesting this experiment, we have now added these results to appendix C.

Based on these observations, we can conclude that the performance gains of CoSe-Co over PGQA are not due to using a different backbone but because CoSe-Co is trained over semantically related sentence-commonsense pairs that enables it to generate contextually more relevant and useful commonsense.

***

> My main concern is about the technical novelty of the proposed method. Compared to the path generator in (Wang et al., 2020b), the difference is that CoSe-Co is T5-based LM rather than GPT-2 and can take the natural sentences as input.

Consider the question- *‘Where could you see an advertisement while reading news?’*. PGQA extracts ‘reading news’ from the question, considers it as the source entity, and pairs it up with a candidate choice ‘television’ as the target entity to generate the path- ```‘read_news  hassubevent  read  relatedto  news  atlocation  television’``` ignoring the context that advertisement is being seen along with reading news and hence it ends up predicting television as answer which is wrong. On the other hand, CoSe-Co takes the question as input and generates the path- ```‘spread_information  _capableof advertisement  atlocation  web_page  usedfor  reading_news’```. Here it can be seen that CoSe-Co considers the entire sentence context, uses the understanding that seeing the advertisement and reading news is happening together and generates path accordingly to relate them with ‘web page’ which is the correct answer. This highlights the fact that considering overall context is crucial and generating commonsense while ignoring this context is a major drawback of PGQA which needs to be addressed.

We would like to emphasize that we design CoSe-Co with the goal of developing a **task-agnostic** commonsense generator that takes into account the **overall context** of the input text. Conditioning on sentences as input to generate relevant commonsense enables us to apply CoSe-Co across various tasks. On the other hand, PGQA is designed **specifically for multi-choice QA** and relies on answer choices and entity extraction for commonsense generation. It extracts entities from text and generates commonsense between entities and answer choices **independent of the overall context** of the question which is a major drawback.

In order to train CoSe-Co, we need a dataset comprising of pairs of natural language sentences and associated commonsense inferences. To create the dataset, we first sample paths from an underlying commonsense KG, and then retrieve sentences from a sentence corpus that are semantically relevant and related to a sampled path. We then use this dataset to train CoSe-Co to generate contextually relevant commonsense paths given an input sentence.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer TrPL (1/2)

content.title: Response to Reviewer TrPL (2/2)
content.comment:
***

> The claimed significant improvement on multi-choice QA is about 3%. However, experimental results in Table 2 show the improvement is only about 0.58% on test split using full training data, compared to QA-GNN. Besides, when using 60% training data, the improvement over PGQA is also incremental.

The claimed improvement of up to 3% on multi-choice QA is over PGQA baseline on using **20% training data** where CoSe-Co achieves an accuracy of 61.2% as compared to 58.25% for PGQA. We would like to highlight that an improvement of ~3% in a very low (20%) training data regime holds even more importance since it signifies that knowledge generated by CoSe-Co helps the QA model to generalize better than the baselines. Further, the improvement over QA-GNN baseline is ~2% in the 20% and 60% training data settings.

***

> The comparison with PGQA is a bit unfair since PGQA is based on GPT-2 (trained on 40 GB text data) while CoSe-Co is based on T5-base (trained on 7 TB).

* We would like to highlight that T5-base is pre-trained on the filtered C4 dataset which is not 7 TB but ~750 GB in size. 7 TB is the size of raw unfiltered C4 dataset and the authors of T5 [1] showed that using it for pre-training results in lesser performance than using the filtered version. Also, compared to GPT-2 (which has ~1.5 billion parameters), T5-base is ~7 times lighter since it comprises ~220 million parameters. 
* Further, we noted that PGQA uses about ~2800K paths to train their path generator while on the other hand, CoSe-Co is trained using just ~290K sentence-path samples (about ~10 times lesser than PGQA). Even then it performs better than PGQA which indicates that the idea of training over semantically related sentence-commonsense pairs helps it to generate more contextually relevant commonsense leading to improvements.

[1] Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, Sharan Narang, Michael Matena, Yanqi Zhou, Wei Li, and Peter J. Liu. Exploring the limits of transfer learning with a unified text-to-text transformer. CoRR, abs/1910.10683, 2019.

***

> In Section 4.2, the ratio of the novel entities in generated paths by CoSe-Co can reach 23.28%, which are not present in training paths. I am curious where these novel entities come from.

During sentence to path training, given a sentence as input, CoSe-Co learns to generate a contextually relevant commonsense path comprising of KG entities connected through relations. Since CoSe-Co is trained by fine-tuning a generative pre-trained language model as the backbone, it transfers the learning and textual knowledge gained during its pre-training to the task of path generation. Hence during inference, it outputs novel natural language phrases and textual concepts as entities (while generating a commonsense path) that are semantically and contextually relevant to the sentence but not present in the KG. As an example, given the sentence - ‘Google maps and other GPS services have replaced what?’, CoSe-Co generates the path - ```‘satellite_gear  hascontext  maps  capableof  help_find_places’``` where ```‘help_find_places’``` is a novel entity not present in KG, yet CoSe-Co generalizes during inference and applies its understanding that maps are typically helpful to find places while generating the path.

***

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer TrPL (2/2)

content.title: Response to Authors
content.comment:
Thank the authors for the backbone experiments and detailed response to my comments. 
***	
I also acknowledge the claim that CoSe-Co is different from PGQA. However, the major difference I can tell between CoSe-Co and PGQA is that the former utilize the entire sentence context to generate commonsense path while the latter only extracts some source entities to produce commonsense path. Moreover, the performance gain of CoSe-Co is small, especially when using full training data.

For the novel entity case, `‘satellite_gear hascontext maps capableof help_find_places’`, I still do not understand why `‘help_find_places’` could be a novel entity, as it is unlikely that the vocabulary of PLM contains `‘help_find_places’`.
***	
Overall, I appreciate the authors' response and raise my score to 5.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Authors

content.title: Response to Reviewer's Reply
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for considering our response and revising the score.

***
> I still do not understand why ```'help_find_places'``` could be a novel entity, as it is unlikely that the vocabulary of PLM contains ```'help_find_places'```.

The PLM’s vocabulary is determined based on a sub-word tokenizer where a word is broken down into frequently occurring tokens that together constitute the word (for eg. ‘playing’ is broken into ‘play’ and ‘ing’). Hence, instead of generating the entire word or phrase together in a single generation step, the generative PLM will sequentially generate the tokens which constitute the phrase ```'help_find_places'``` across multiple consecutive decoding steps. The subword tokens are present in the PLM vocabulary and not the entire phrase.

***

**Human Evaluation** : Further, we study the difference in the quality of generated commonsense between CoSe-Co and PGQA by conducting a human evaluation and found that knowledge generated by CoSe-Co is significantly more contextually relevant than PGQA. For human study, we presented evaluators with questions from CSQA dataset along with corresponding commonsense paths generated by CoSe-Co and PGQA in an anonymized manner. We asked them to compare the paths based on their contextual relevance with the complete sentence and rate which path is better. We also provided them an option to mark neutral in case none of the paths is clearly better than the other for a given sample. A total of 150 questions samples were randomly sampled from the test set and presented to 6 evaluators (25 samples each). Following are our observations:

* Number of samples where CoSe-Co is better: 62 (41.33% of 150 samples)
* Number of samples where PGQA is better: 38 (25.33% of 150 samples)
* Number of samples where both are of similar quality: 50 (33.33% of 150 samples)
 
This shows that commonsense generated by CoSe-Co is found to be more relevant in human evaluation. Also, if we exclude neutral samples and consider the 100 samples where the path generated by one of the two methods is found to be better, CoSe-Co’s paths are found to be more relevant in 62 samples (62% of 100 samples) while PGQA’s paths are more relevant in 38 samples (38% of 100 samples). We have now added this human study to qualitative analysis in Appendix A in the updated draft.

content.title: General Response to Reviewers and ACs (1/2) - Revision Details
content.comment:
We would like to thank all the reviewers for their valuable feedback and suggestions for improving the paper. 
Here we summarise the main improvements made in the draft.

* Performed experiments to analyze the effect of replacing the backbone language model of CoSe-Co from T5-base to GPT-2. The results and discussion have been added to Appendix C.
* Qualitative comparisons with baselines for multi-choice QA were present in Appendix A. We have now added a discussion to the main paper also through one of these examples (in Section 4.3) to qualitatively highlight the key differences and reasons for improvements.
* Added Figure 3 to demonstrate each step in sentence-path paired dataset creation through illustrations. Further elaborated the intuition behind the choice of query templates (Section 3.1). 
* Added T5 baselines for multi-choice QA to Table 2.
* Refined the writing according to reviewers’ comments and enhanced details (such as path quality analysis in Section 4.2, etc.) for better clarity.

We would also like to discuss the experiments done to explore the effect of changing the backbone language model of CoSe-Co from T5-base to GPT-2. We train GPT-2 using the same sentence-path dataset as we used for T5-base by providing it as input the sentence followed by a [SEP] token and adapting GPT-2 to generate the corresponding path. Additionally, we also experiment with replacing the language model in PGQA from GPT-2 to T5-base. The following table summarises the results obtained for multi-choice QA on CSQA.

| Method                 	| IHDev 	| IHTest 	|               |
|------------------------	|-------	|--------	|------------	|
| RoBERTa-large  (w/o KG)         		| 73.07 (±0.45)| 68.69 (±0.56) |
| + PGQA (w/ GPT-2)      	| 77.53 (±0.47) | 71.19 (±0.49) |
| + CoSe-Co (w/ GPT-2)   	| **77.90** (±0.37) | **72.67** (±0.18)|
|                        	|       	|        	|            	|
| + PGQA (w/ T5-base)    	| 77.56 (±0.32)| 71.31 (±0.44)| 
| + CoSe-Co (w/ T5-base) 	| **78.15** (±0.23)| **72.87** (±0.31) |

Based on these observations, we can conclude that the performance gains of CoSe-Co over PGQA are not due to using a different backbone but because CoSe-Co is trained over semantically related sentence-commonsense pairs that enables it to generate contextually more relevant and useful commonsense.
